transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
President Trump has arrived in Manila, where he'll attend a summit in the Philippines ahead
of this week's meetings in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President
Vladimir Putin, and PR's Franco Ordonez reports.
President Trump will meet with Southeast Asian leaders who are gathering for the ASEAN summit,
but much of the attention will be on the second half of the trip when Trump travels to China
to meet with Presidents Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Well, we're going to be talking about denuclearization.
We'll talk about Iran.
We have Iran in very good shape.
We'll talk about Iran in a little bit.
We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine.
Ukraine's losing.
Ukraine, Russia's losing 25,000 soldiers.
Come on, Trump.
We'll be coming back.
We'll be coming back.
We'll be coming back.
We'll all be talking about economic and trade.
Trump suggested he may also meet with Kim Jong-un of North Korea, Franco Ordonez and
PR News, the White House.
The Baltic nation of Estonia says it will soon close its border crossings with Russia,
and PR's Charles Maines in Moscow says the government accuses Russia of sabotage.
The closure goes into effect December 1st and follows what Estonia says was a foiled
plot by Russian security services to detonate explosives at a local drone manufacturing
plant.
The Kremlin has denied the charge and condemned Estonia's border closure, which is the latest
to complicate land travel from Russia into Europe.
Finland closed its border transit with Russia in 2023 amid a surge in migrants it blamed
on Moscow, and closing at other points such as Latvia and northern Norway remain limited.
The throttled land traffic comes as Europe has accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks
on its infrastructure in a bid to undermine the European public's support for Ukraine.
Charles Maines, NPR News, Moscow.
Microsoft says it's learning more about what caused last week's global outage affecting
millions of users in more than 70 countries.
Here's NPR's Andrea Hsu.
In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna said a latent
defect combined with increased load and a reduced server capacity were to blame for
the outage, which began Thursday and spilled into Friday.
The failure unfolded rapidly over just a couple hours.
At one point, the previously unknown defect had rendered more than 80% of Microsoft's
servers unresponsive.
Services weren't fully restored until early Saturday.
Lamanna explained the recovery took longer than usual because servers came back online.
They were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic.
He once again apologized for the disruption caused to all Microsoft customers.
Andrea Hsu, NPR News.
United Airlines says it doesn't believe yesterday's systemwide outage that delayed departing flights
for more than 90 minutes was the result of a cybersecurity issue.
This is NPR News from Washington.
JPMorgan Chase says hackers were not responsible for yesterday's technical issue that affected
thousands of customers, as well as several other banks.
Many people had trouble accessing online accounts and transferring money through Zelle.
The issue was blamed on a software bug and appears to be resolved this morning.
Gasoline and diesel prices continue falling across the U.S.
AAA says regular now averages $3.78 a gallon.
The price has dropped about 20 cents in the last week, and NPR's Willa Rubin says the
cost of diesel has fallen to less than $6 a gallon.
Diesel is dropping because of another drop in crude prices.
Crude is getting cheaper because more oil is getting out of the Middle East, so supply
and demand.
And here's why lower diesel prices matter.
Diesel is the workhorse of the economy.
Much of the nation's farming and trucking runs on diesel.
When diesel goes up over time, so does the price of just about everything.
So this is a counterweight to inflation.
But a gallon of diesel still costs more than $2 more than a year ago.
Willa Rubin, NPR News.
President Trump's choice to serve as Secretary of the Navy is scheduled to appear before
the Senate Armed Services Committee today.
Acting Secretary Hung Kao is expected to face many questions about the war with Iran, as
he seeks the Navy's top civilian job.
Kao is a combat veteran who would need a waiver from Congress to serve, having left active
duty less than seven years ago.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: President Trump arrives in Manila for ASEAN summit before planned China meetings with Xi and Putin
Estonia to close border crossings with Russia from December 1, citing foiled sabotage plot
Microsoft explains global outage caused by latent defect and server capacity overload
United Airlines says last week's systemwide outage was not caused by a cybersecurity issue
JPMorgan Chase says hackers not responsible for technical issue affecting customers and other banks
Gasoline and diesel prices keep falling nationwide, with regular averaging $3.78 a gallon
Trump's Navy Secretary nominee Hung Kao faces Senate Armed Services Committee hearing today
